question: Move the AED at P.S. 110 Florence Nightingale into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: P.S. 110 Florence Nightingale (School, ZIP 10002) has a registered AED at "gym by nurse's office; across stair D".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.45 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 3 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 6 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists FDNY Engine 15, a fire station normally staffed around the clock, 317 m away: a possible alternative host for a 24/7 AED.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving P.S. 110's AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet addresses a genuine gap in emergency access. The school's current location is reachable only 55 of 168 hours weekly during the school year [E2][E3], yet the area experienced 1.45 cardiac-arrest calls annually during hours when all nearby AEDs were closed [E4]. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED correlates with 66.5% survival versus 43.0% without [E7]. While Engine 15 sits 317 meters away [E8], it remains unknown whether that station currently hosts a 24/7 AED. A street-wall cabinet would eliminate the school-hours constraint and ensure round-the-clock availability for the neighborhood's actual emergency pattern.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The proposal rests on incomplete information that undermines confidence in moving this particular AED. While the survival data is compelling [E7], we don't know the cabinet's cost, vandalism risk, or whether the school already permits after-hours access [E9]—factors that could make this inefficient. More critically, Engine 15 sits only 317 meters away and is normally staffed around the clock [E8], yet we haven't confirmed whether it already hosts a 24/7 AED. Before relocating school equipment, we should verify what's actually available at that fire station. The 1.45 annual calls [E4] are significant but we lack precise location data—they're ZIP-code level only [E9], so we can't confirm they're all within two minutes of P.S. 110's current spot. Exploring the fire station option first seems prudent.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic is right that Engine 15 deserves investigation first—we should confirm whether it already hosts a 24/7 AED before committing to relocate school equipment. However, the skeptic's caution about ZIP-code precision cuts both ways. Yes, we lack exact call locations [E9], but the data we do have is stark: the area ranks 3 of 100 NYC schools for cardiac arrests occurring when all nearby AEDs were shut [E4]. Even if some of those 1.45 annual calls fell outside P.S. 110's two-minute radius, the pattern shows a genuine access gap. Checking Engine 15 is sensible, but if that station lacks a 24/7 AED or proves administratively unavailable, the school cabinet becomes the practical solution to a documented survival problem [E7].

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The Advocate makes a fair point that Engine 15 deserves investigation first, but their framing glosses over a critical gap. We know Engine 15 is normally staffed around the clock [E8], yet we don't know whether it already hosts a 24/7 AED or could readily accept one. Before we incur costs and risks moving school equipment—cabinet expenses, vandalism exposure, and potential disruption to the school [E9]—we need that answer. The ranking of 3 of 100 schools [E4] is concerning, but it doesn't tell us whether P.S. 110 is the best place to solve it. A fire station designed for emergency response might be the more natural, cost-effective host. Verify Engine 15's capacity first.

verdict.summary: Genuine access gap exists (1.45 annual calls during AED-closed hours, rank 3 of 100 schools). Survival benefit proven (66.5% vs 43.0%). However, Engine 15 fire station 317m away with 24/7 staffing must be confirmed as AED host before relocating school equipment.
verdict.strongestFor: 1.45 annual cardiac arrests during all-AED-closed hours [E4]; 66.5% survival with public AED shock [E7]; current location reachable only 55/168 weekly hours [E3].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Engine 15 fire station 317m away normally staffed 24/7 [E8] but unknown if it hosts 24/7 AED; unknown cabinet cost, vandalism risk, school access policy [E9]; call locations ZIP-level only, not confirmed within P.S. 110's two-minute radius [E9].
verdict.nextStep: Confirm whether FDNY Engine 15 currently hosts or can accept a 24/7 AED before relocating P.S. 110 equipment.
